title: Aggregate a Markov chain's state space by Kullback-Leibler minimization — aggregateStates
code: # A chain aggregated into two macro-states {a,b}/{c,d} where, in addition # to being strongly lumpable, "a" and "b" also split their probability # *within* each destination block identically (0.1/0.1 and 0.4/0.4): this # stronger property is what makes the divergence exactly zero (see # Details for a lumpable-but-nonzero counterexample). statesNames <- c("a", "b", "c", "d") P <- matrix(c(0.1, 0.1, 0.4, 0.4,               0.1, 0.1, 0.4, 0.4,               0.3, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2,               0.3, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 4,             dimnames = list(statesNames, statesNames)) mc <- new("markovchain", states = statesNames, transitionMatrix = P)  result <- aggregateStates(mc, k = 2) result$partition #> $Macro_1 #> [1] "a" "b" #>  #> $Macro_2 #> [1] "c" "d" #>  result$klDivergence # zero up to rounding #> [1] -1.110223e-16

code: # A directed 3-cycle is as far from reversible as a chain gets: it only # ever moves one way round. Its closest reversible approximation is the # undirected random walk on the same triangle. statesNames <- c("a", "b", "c") cycle3 <- new("markovchain", states = statesNames,   transitionMatrix = matrix(c(0, 1, 0,                               0, 0, 1,                               1, 0, 0), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 3,                             dimnames = list(statesNames, statesNames))) is.reversible(cycle3) #> [1] FALSE  approximation <- closestReversible(cycle3) approximation$chain #> Unnamed Markov chain (closest reversible)  #>  A  3 - dimensional discrete Markov Chain defined by the following states:  #>  a, b, c  #>  The transition matrix  (by rows)  is defined as follows:  #>     a   b   c #> a 0.0 0.5 0.5 #> b 0.5 0.0 0.5 #> c 0.5 0.5 0.0 #>  is.reversible(approximation$chain) #> [1] TRUE approximation$distance #> [1] 1.224745  # The nearest reversible chain in the Frobenius norm (needs quadprog), # first with the stationary distribution held fixed, then free. if (requireNamespace("quadprog", quietly = TRUE)) {   P <- new("markovchain", states = letters[1:4], transitionMatrix = matrix(     c(0.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.15, 0.7, 0.1,       0.3, 0.05, 0.25, 0.4, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.2), 4, byrow = TRUE,     dimnames = list(letters[1:4], letters[1:4])))   closestReversible(P)$frobeniusDistance   closestReversible(P, norm = "frobenius")$distance   set.seed(1)   free <- closestReversible(P, "free", norm = "frobenius")   free$distance   free$stationaryDistribution } #>          a          b          c          d  #> 0.20622910 0.29041450 0.40357449 0.09978191

title: Entropy rate of a Markov chain — entropyRate
text: row-stochastic transition matrix \(P\) stationary distribution \(\pi\), entropy rate $$H = -\sum_i \pi_i \sum_j p_{ij}\log_b(p_{ij}),$$ zero-probability transitions contributing zero continuity. stationary first-order Markov chain, entropy rate equals conditional entropy \(H(X_{t+1}\mid X_t)\). Irreducibility guarantees unique stationary distribution; aperiodicity required. Reducible chains may admit multiple stationary distributions therefore different entropy rates. method rejects rather silently selecting one stationary distribution. Transitions probability zero ignored, implementing standard convention \(0\log(0)=0\) without evaluating log(0). stationary-distribution computation dominates running time. stationary distribution available, evaluating entropy rate takes \(O(n^2)\) time \(O(n^2)\) temporary memory dense \(n\)-state transition matrix.

title: Markov chain approximating a continuous transition kernel by quadrature — fitFunction
text: nodes \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\) weights \(w_1, \ldots, w_n\) rule \(\int g(y)\,dy\), transition matrix $$P_{ij} = \frac{w_j f(y_i, y_j)}{\sum_{k} w_k f(y_i, y_k)}.$$ \(f(x, \cdot)\) transition density continuous process, \(\sum_j P_{ij} h(y_j)\) approximates \(E[h(Y_{t+1}) \mid Y_t = y_i]\) every smooth \(h\), normalization corrects mass lost outside nodes. kernel need integrate one: values nodes matter. rules, positive weights: "gauss-legendre": Gauss-Legendre nodes, exact polynomials degree \(2n - 1\). good default smooth kernels bounded interval. "gauss-chebyshev": Gauss-Chebyshev nodes first kind, \(t_k = -\cos((2k - 1)\pi / (2n))\) \([-1, 1]\), weights \((\pi/n)\sqrt{1 - t_k^2}\) plain integral. exact \(g(t) = q(t)/\sqrt{1 - t^2}\) \(q\) polynomial degree \(2n - 1\), suits kernels kind behaviour end points. "fejer": Fejer's first rule, Chebyshev nodes weights integrate exactly every polynomial degree \(n - 1\). rule PyDTMC calls "gauss-chebyshev". "gauss-hermite": Gauss-Hermite nodes normal distribution \(N(\code{mean}, \code{sd}^2)\), processes real line. weights plain integral probability weights divided normal density nodes. AR(1) density method Tauchen Hussey (1991); see tauchenHussey. "trapezoid" "simpson": equally spaced nodes including end points; Simpson's rule needs odd size. "midpoint": centres size equal cells. Newton-Cotes rules high order offered, weights become negative give negative probabilities. row whose kernel values zero nodes (process reach node ) stops function error: PyDTMC replaces row uniform distribution, invents transitions; interval, number nodes kernel changed instead. kernel, interval number nodes, "gauss-legendre", "fejer", "trapezoid" "simpson" rules give matrices PyDTMC 10.0.0 ("gauss-legendre", "gauss-chebyshev", "trapezoid-rule" "simpson-rule"); PyDTMC's midpoint rule ("newton-cotes") ignores lower end interval.

title: Check whether a Markov chain is reversible — is.reversible
text: chain transition matrix \(P\) stationary distribution \(\pi\) reversible $$\pi_i P_{ij} = \pi_j P_{ji} \quad \text{every } ,j.$$ Intuitively, started chain \(\pi\) watched long run , running recorded sequence states backwards look statistically identical running forwards: stationarity, "flow" probability \(\) \(j\) exactly balances flow \(j\) \(\). irreducibility required, aperiodicity: detailed balance purely algebraic condition \(P\) \(\pi\) perfectly well defined periodic chains . example, simple random walk undirected graph (moving uniformly random neighbour) always reversible, whether happens periodic. 2-state irreducible chain always reversible: two states, single detailed balance equation \(\pi_1 P_{12} = \pi_2 P_{21}\) just restatement stationarity equation \(\pi P = \pi\), holds automatically. Every reversible chain real spectrum (eigenvalues \(P\) real), slem spectralGap especially easy interpret reversible chains: complex-conjugate eigenvalue pairs reason . implementation calls steadyStates , compares two triangles flow matrix \(\pi_i P_{ij}\). time complexity dominated steadyStates(), plus additional \(O(n^2)\) comparison dense \(n\)-state transition matrix. supports row- column-stochastic storage.

title: Kemeny's constant of a Markov chain — kemenyConstant
text: row-stochastic transition matrix \(P\), let \(\pi\) unique stationary distribution define $$Z = (- P + \mathbf{1}\pi^T)^{-1}.$$ hitting times defined \(T_j = \inf\{n \ge 0: X_n=j\}\), \(m_{jj}=0\), function returns $$K = \sum_j \pi_j m_{ij} = \mathrm{tr}(Z)-1.$$ value depend starting state \(\). Irreducibility sufficient; aperiodicity required. Reducible chains can multiple stationary distributions rejected. references instead put mean first-return time \(m_{jj}=1/\pi_j\) diagonal. convention corresponding stationary weighted sum \(K+1\), \(K\). function uses zero-diagonal hitting-time convention, consistently meanFirstPassageTime(). implementation uses dense LAPACK solve fundamental matrix \(Z\). time complexity \(O(n^3)\) memory use \(O(n^2)\), expected dense exact computation. supports row- column-stochastic storage.

title: Build a lazy version of a Markov chain — lazyChain
text: transition matrix \(P\) (whichever storage convention object already uses) laziness parameter \(\alpha\[0,1]\), lazy chain's transition matrix $$L = \alpha + (1-\alpha) P.$$ Laziness standard device forcing aperiodicity without changing chain can go stationary distribution: \(L\) stationary distribution \(P\) (\(\pi P=\pi\) \(\pi L = \alpha\pi + (1-\alpha)\pi P =     \pi\)), communicating classes, since \(L_{ij}>0 \iff P_{ij}>0\) \(\ne j\). \(0<\alpha<1\), \(L\) aperiodic even \(P\) periodic, \(L_{ii}=\alpha>0\) every state \(\) rules period greater \(1\). mixingTime, requires aperiodicity, often applied lazyChain(object) rather periodic object directly (see mixingTime's documentation rejects periodic chains outright rather lazifying automatically). Every non-trivial eigenvalue \(L\) \(\alpha + (1-\alpha)\lambda\) corresponding eigenvalue \(\lambda\) \(P\): laziness shrinks whole non-trivial spectrum towards \(\alpha\), slem impliedTimescales generally get worse (mixing gets slower) alpha increases towards 1. \(\alpha=0\) returns \(P\) unchanged; \(\alpha=1\) returns identity matrix (chain never moves).

text: model Either "moran" "wright-fisher", selecting reproduction scheme generates transition matrix. n single integer least 2: (constant) population size. chain n + 1 states, \(0,1,\ldots,n\), possible mutant-allele counts. s single finite number greater -1: selection coefficient. mutant allele's fitness relative wild-type \(1+s\) (s = 0 neutral drift, s > 0 favours mutant, -1 < s < 0 disfavours ). u single number \([0,1]\): backward mutation rate, mutant wild-type. title: Build a population-genetics Markov chain (Moran or Wright-Fisher) — populationGeneticsModel
text: Moran model. step one individual chosen reproduce (probability proportional type's relative fitness, mutant fitness \(r=1+s\) wild-type fitness \(1\)) one individual, chosen uniformly random, dies replaced offspring, mutates probability u v depending parent's type. interior state \(\) (\(0<<n\)), writing \(r_i=(1+s)\) \(m_i=n-\), $$P_{,-1}=\frac{}{n}\cdot\frac{r_i u + m_i(1-v)}{r_i+m_i},\qquad   P_{,+1}=\frac{m_i}{n}\cdot\frac{r_i(1-u) + m_i v}{r_i+m_i},$$ \(P_{ii}\) remainder. Wright-Fisher model. Generations discrete non-overlapping: interior state \(\), mutant-allele frequency \(k=/n\) first updated mutation, \(p=k(1-u)+(1-k)v\), viability selection, \(p'=\min\bigl(p(1+s)/(1+ps),\,1\bigr)\), next generation's mutant count \(\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p')\)-distributed: \(P_{ij}=\binom{n}{j}p'^{\,j}(1-p')^{n-j}\). constructions follow PyDTMC's population_genetics_model, two deliberate differences. First, function uses mutant relative fitness \(1+s\) models (PyDTMC's Moran implementation instead uses \(1-s\), positive s favours wild-type rather mutant, opposite Wright-Fisher convention usual textbook one). Second, mutation terms: u != v probability \(P_{,-1}\) follows description model (mutant parent wild-type offspring probability u, wild-type parent probability 1-v), whereas PyDTMC uses \(r_i v\) place \(r_i u\) numerator, makes chain depend two alleles labelled; u = v (default) two coincide. s = 0 u = v two packages' Moran chains identical; otherwise differ construction, design (s, keep meaning consistent "moran" "wright-fisher" within package). u, v shrink 0, reduce classical drift-chains absorbing loss/fixation states, going back Wright (1931) Moran (1958); see Ewens (2004) modern textbook treatment .

Mathematical Proceedings Cambridge Philosophical Society, 54(1), 60-71. Ewens, W. J. (2004). Mathematical Population Genetics : Theoretical Introduction (2nd ed.). Springer.

title: Discretize an AR(1) process into a Markov chain (Rouwenhorst's method) — rouwenhorst
text: Approximates stationary first-order autoregressive process $$y_t = (1-\rho)\alpha + \rho y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad   \varepsilon_t \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$$ finite-state Markov chain, following Rouwenhorst (1995). Unlike tauchen, grid-width parameter needed method remains accurate rho close \(\pm 1\).

title: Discretize an AR(1) process into a Markov chain (Rouwenhorst's method) — rouwenhorst
text: alpha single finite number: unconditional mean process. sigma single finite positive number: standard deviation innovation \(\varepsilon_t\). rho single number \((-1,1)\): autocorrelation (persistence) process. size single integer least 2: number grid points (states) discretized chain.

title: Discretize an AR(1) process into a Markov chain (Rouwenhorst's method) — rouwenhorst
text: named list two elements, chain states, form returned tauchen.

title: Discretize an AR(1) process into a Markov chain (Rouwenhorst's method) — rouwenhorst
text: grid \(n=\code{size}\) evenly spaced points spanning \([\alpha-\psi,\ \alpha+\psi]\) \(\psi=\sigma_y\sqrt{n-1}\), \(\sigma_y=\sigma/\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\) process's unconditional standard deviation: particular width (rather fixed multiple \(\sigma_y\) tauchen) method needs order match AR(1)'s variance first-order autocorrelation exactly every size, including rho near \(\pm1\). transition matrix built recursively. Let \(\theta=(1+\rho)/2\) , two states, $$\Theta_2 = \begin{pmatrix}\theta & 1-\theta\\ 1-\theta & \theta\end{pmatrix}.$$ \(m\) states (\(2<m\le n\)), form \(m\times m\) matrix $$\Theta_m = \theta\begin{pmatrix}\Theta_{m-1} & 0\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}   + (1-\theta)\begin{pmatrix}0 & \Theta_{m-1}\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}   + (1-\theta)\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\ \Theta_{m-1} & 0\end{pmatrix}   + \theta\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0\\ 0 & \Theta_{m-1}\end{pmatrix},$$ divide every interior row (first last) \(2\) restore row-stochasticity, since rows receive contributions two four corner blocks . Rouwenhorst's method reproduces AR(1)'s unconditional variance lag-1 autocorrelation \(\rho\) exactly, every size (Kopecky Suen (2010) find outperforms tauchen several methods across persistence range typically seen quarterly macroeconomic actuarial time series, e.g. discretized short-rate inflation processes reserving ALM work).

Kopecky, K. . Suen, R. M. H. (2010). Finite state Markov-chain approximations highly persistent processes. Review Economic Dynamics, 13(3), 701-714.

title: Second largest eigenvalue modulus (SLEM) of a Markov chain — slem
text: row-stochastic transition matrix \(P\), let \(1=\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_n\) eigenvalues. Perron-Frobenius theorem irreducible chain \(\lambda_1=1\) algebraic multiplicity one, \(|\lambda_k|\le 1\) every \(k\). SLEM $$\mathrm{SLEM} = \max_{k>1} |\lambda_k|.$$ irreducibility required, aperiodicity. chain periodic, least one non-trivial eigenvalue also modulus one (e.g. \(\lambda=-1\) 2-cycle), slem() correctly returns 1 rather rejecting chain: periodic chain genuinely contract towards stationary distribution, SLEM = 1 reflects. Repeated complex non-trivial eigenvalues handled modulus Mod(), complex-conjugate pairs contribute value ties need broken. implementation calls eigen() .values = TRUE, never computes eigenvectors. time complexity \(O(n^3)\) memory use \(O(n^2)\) dense \(n\)-state transition matrix. supports row- column-stochastic storage.

Returning actual levels alongside chain, rather generic state labels "1", "2", ..., deliberate: whole point discretizing AR(1) process usually numeric work levels (e.g. plugging pricing formula), re-deriving grid alpha, sigma, rho k second time hand extra work place --one rounding mismatch creep .

title: Discretize an AR(1) process into a Markov chain (Tauchen's method) — tauchen
text: grid \(n=\code{size}\) evenly spaced points \(y_1<\cdots<y_n\) spanning \([\alpha-k\sigma_y,\ \alpha+k\sigma_y]\), half-spacing \(w=(y_n-y_1)/(2(n-1))\). Writing \(\Phi\) standard normal CDF, transition probabilities grid point \(y_i\) $$P_{i1} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{y_1-(1-\rho)\alpha-\rho y_i+w}{\sigma}\right),$$ $$P_{} = 1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{y_n-(1-\rho)\alpha-\rho y_i-w}{\sigma}\right),$$ $$P_{ij} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{y_j-(1-\rho)\alpha-\rho y_i+w}{\sigma}\right) -   \Phi\!\left(\frac{y_j-(1-\rho)\alpha-\rho y_i-w}{\sigma}\right),   \quad 1<j<n,$$ .e. probability \(y_t\) (normal draw centred AR(1) conditional mean) lands half-open bin around \(y_j\), two end bins extended \(\pm\infty\) rows sum exactly \(1\). Tauchen's method simple fast (\(O(n^2)\) normal CDF evaluations) grid width fixed k regardless size: coarse grid (small size) -resolves bulk distribution, rho close \(\pm1\) true unconditional variance large sensitive k. See rouwenhorst alternative tends match persistence near-unit-root processes accurately needs arbitrary grid-width parameter.

text: alpha single finite number: unconditional mean process. sigma single finite positive number: standard deviation innovation \(\varepsilon_t\). rho single number \((-1,1)\): autocorrelation (persistence) process. size single integer least 2: number grid points (states) discretized chain. sigmaWeight standard deviation \(\hat\sigma\) normal distribution defining nodes chosen: "conditional" (default, Tauchen Hussey's original choice) uses \(\hat\sigma = \sigma\); "unconditional" uses \(\hat\sigma = \sigma_y = \sigma/\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\); "floden" uses Floden's compromise \(\hat\sigma = w\sigma + (1-w)\sigma_y\) \(w = 1/2 + \rho/4\).

text: sequence defines observable \(f\) states: \(f_j\) number times state \(j\) occurs . \(f\) sequence1, \(g\) sequence2, transition matrix \(P\) stationary distribution \(\pi\), $$\mathrm{timeCorrelations}(t) = \sum_i \pi_i f_i (P^t g)_i =   E_\pi[f(X_0) g(X_t)],$$ , initial distribution \(\mu\), $$\mathrm{timeRelaxations}(t) = \mu P^t f = E_\mu[f(X_t)].$$ ergodic chain, converge \(t\) grows, \(E_\pi[f] E_\pi[g]\) \(E_\pi[f]\) respectively, speed governed second largest eigenvalue modulus (slem). powers \(P\) applied repeated multiplication, repeated squaring long lags, never eigendecomposition. PyDTMC 9.0.0 switches eigendecomposition soon lag exceeds number states; since left right eigenvectors biorthonormal \(P\) complex eigenvalues, returns wrong values every lag chains (tests function include one, whose correct values checked numpy). timeCorrelations needs unique stationary distribution, .e. exactly one recurrent class, stops otherwise (PyDTMC returns None). timeRelaxations defined every chain; unlike PyDTMC, require unique stationary distribution.

text: object markovchain object least 2 states. boundaryCondition Either: string "absorbing": first last state become absorbing (\(P_{11}=1\), \(P_{nn}=1\)); string "reflecting": first state moves second certainty last state moves second--last certainty (\(P_{12}=1\), \(P_{n,n-1}=1\)); single number \(\beta\[0,1]\), semi-reflecting case: first state stays probability \(1-\beta\) moves second state probability \(\beta\) (\(P_{11}=1-\beta\), \(P_{12}=\beta\)), symmetrically last state stays probability \(1-\beta\) moves second--last probability \(\beta\). \(\beta=0\) absorbing case \(\beta=1\) reflecting case.
